  • A remote access trojan that can deliver additional .NET payloads, while using Google Drive, OneDrive, and Yandex.Disk for command-and-control (C2) to blend in with regular enterprise workflows. It's also equipped to harvest system information and upload files of interest.
  • A malicious DLL dubbed OxiDLLRunner that's sideloaded by the legitimate "googleupdate.exe" binary, which is also delivered by the bootkit. The DLL decrypts and launches a Rust payload that communicates with "archivetj[.]com" to receive and execute more DLL plugins.

BlackX's connections to APT41 stem from an ESET report in June 2026, which documented FishMonger's use of a Windows backdoor called SprySOCKS in attacks targeting government entities in Honduras, Taiwan, Thailand, and Pakistan between 2023 and 2024. FishMonger, also tracked as Aquatic Panda and Earth Lusca, is assessed to be operating under the APT41 umbrella.

The Slovakian cybersecurity company said it had found "limited indications" that some versions of the backdoor may feature a UEFI bootkit component likely exploiting CVE‑2023‑24932, another security feature bypass vulnerability linked to BlackLotus.

An interesting overlap is the presence of the "xdd" string in BlackX and the kernel implant used by FishMonger, raising the possibility that the UEFI bootkit used in those attacks is none other than BlackX. The second clue that points to China-aligned hackers is the use of DLL sideloading to deploy the payloads – a pattern that's extremely common among threat actors of Chinese origin.

"By adapting a commercial crimeware tool, the group could bypass procedures intended to protect the Windows boot processes," Kucherin said. "This hybrid approach proves that sophisticated adversaries do not need to reinvent the wheel to establish persistent, invisible control over high-value networks."

item.title: CISA Flags Two Actively Exploited Critical Flaws in Collabora Online and Arista VeloCloud (2026)
item.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added two vulnerabilities impacting Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server and Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing reports of active exploitation in the wild.

The critical-severity vulnerabilities are listed below -

  • CVE-2026-110447 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An operating system command injection vulnerability in Collabora Online – Built-in CODE Server (aka richdocumentscode) when used within the NextCloud platform that could allow remote code execution via "proxy.php" when the CODE local document server isn't running. (Fixed in September 2026 in version 26.4.303)
  • CVE-2026-114625 (CVSS score: 9.9) - An SQL injection vulnerability in on-premise versions of Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator that could allow a remote attacker to access privileged internal functionality. (Fixed in October 2026  in versions 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10, and 6.4.2.12)

As reported by The Hacker News, threat actors have been observed exploiting CVE-2026-110447 to backdoor Nextcloud servers with a web shell so as to conduct reconnaissance and search for credential stores, password manager artifacts, and cryptocurrency wallets.

As for CVE-2026-114625, successful exploitation requires an attacker to have network access to the VCO web interface and a valid authenticated session on the VCO portal. The minimum user role required is Enterprise Read Only.

Although Arista has acknowledged that the vulnerability is "known to be actively exploited," it has not attributed the activity to a particular threat actor or provided technical details on how the vulnerability is being exploited and what actions the attackers took after privilege escalation. The company also has not disclosed the number of affected organizations.

However, it has shared two IP addresses geolocated to Japan as responsible for driving the activity -

  • 74.82.197[.]86
  • 38.54.50[.]151

CVE-2026-114625 is the third vulnerability in the same product to have been weaponized in the wild since July 2026, following CVE-2026-16812 (CVSS score: 10.0) and CVE-2026-93952 (CVSS score: 10.0).

In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by October 26, 2026, to secure their networks.

item.title: Researchers Push Over 2 Million Updates to Remotely Disable Popcorn Time Updater That Could Fuel a Botnet (2026)
item.description:
Between November 2025 and March 2026, the Dutch security firm Eye Security pushed more than 2 million updates to computers it did not own to switch off a background updater that it said could have allowed an outsider to take over the machine.

The updater belongs to Time4Popcorn, an abandoned copy of Popcorn Time, a free app that streamed pirated films and TV over BitTorrent.

Popcorn Time was popular about a decade ago, and the original shut down in 2014, but several copies kept running under the same name. A separate, legal project that took the Popcorn Time name in early 2025 is unrelated to it.

Eye Security, which monitors client networks for threats, found the updater during a routine threat hunt: a program called Updater.exe on one client's laptop kept trying to reach a web address that was no longer registered.

The firm registered the address itself to see what would connect, and about 50 requests a second poured in. It later laid out the operation, which it named Operation IXIM, in a write-up and a talk at Hack.lu on October 22.

Over six months, those requests carried more than 3.8 million different hardware IDs. The IDs proved an unreliable way to count machines, because some Windows PCs shared one and some Macs changed theirs, so Eye revised its estimate to 2.5 to 3 million Windows computers and 250,000 to 350,000 Macs.

The updater ran in the background on Windows and Mac from the moment the computer started. It checked for new versions over an unencrypted connection and installed whatever it was sent, at the highest privilege level, called SYSTEM on Windows and root on Mac, without checking who sent it.

Because the web addresses it called had been abandoned, Eye said, anyone who registered the right one could have served their own program to every machine still calling it.

On a machine with that access, an attacker could install ransomware, steal saved passwords, or pull the computer into a botnet, Eye said. Mapping a sample of the connecting addresses, the firm said it saw home users around the world, as well as machines on government, military, and corporate networks, though it added that it is "hard to draw conclusions" from that.

Eye had disclosed the flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-30612, in June. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency rates it 9.8 out of 10. It affects three versions of the Time4Popcorn software:

  • Windows, up to and including 6.2.1.18
  • Mac, up to and including 6.2.1.17
  • Android, up to and including 3.5.0.173

Turning the Updater Against Itself

With no company left to fix the software and no patch coming, Eye decided to use the updater against itself. After taking legal advice, it served the machines an update that does one thing: it stops and disables the updater, deleting no files and collecting nothing.

Eye compared the step to Operation Ladybird in 2021, when Dutch police pushed an update to computers infected with the Emotet botnet to disable the malware on them.

The difference, Eye said, is that Emotet's victims never chose to be infected, while Popcorn Time's users installed the app themselves. Still, the firm said, "none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years."

Soon after the updates began, someone uploaded Eye's update to VirusTotal, and antivirus engines started flagging it as malware, a fair description of a program that disables a Windows service. Because every product that blocked it left the vulnerable updater running, Eye reworked the update until only one scanner continued to flag it.

By December 2025, Eye had updated more than 1 million systems and cut the traffic to its web addresses by about 90 percent. By March 1, it was sending about 5,000 updates a day, a 98 percent reduction. Judging the remaining numbers too small to interest a botnet operator, Eye stopped, having sent more than 2 million update downloads in all.

In late March, Eye handed the 15 web addresses it controlled to the Shadowserver Foundation, a non-profit that takes abandoned and malicious domains out of circulation, so a trusted party would hold them rather than Eye.

Public registration records for one of them, popcorntimeupd[.]xyz, now point to Shadowserver's sinkhole servers, with a transfer dated March 20, 2026. Other addresses the updater calls were never Eye's to take and remain with outside owners, the firm said, so machines that reach those are still exposed.

Eye found no sign that anyone else was serving code through the addresses: the ones already registered by other people were parked or up for sale, not pushing updates to the machines calling them. The flaw is not listed in CISA's catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities as of October 23, 2026.

What Popcorn Time Users Should Do

Switching off the updater does not make the app safe. Eye said Popcorn Time runs on a 2014 browser engine with its security sandbox turned off, loads content over unencrypted connections, and pulls in code from other abandoned web addresses.

Eye registered those abandoned addresses too, which it said would have let it run its own code on every machine that opened the app. It did not, but it built a working proof of concept, so the risk is real. The update only changed the updater, so the rest of the app remains dangerous for anyone who keeps using Popcorn Time.

Eye's advice is to uninstall Popcorn Time. The updater can also be turned off by hand: on Windows with two commands that stop and disable its "Update service," and on a Mac with one that unloads the PT.updd helper. Removing the app is the safer step, because disabling the updater leaves the rest of it in place.

  • Windows: sc.exe stop "Update service"
  • Windows: sc.exe config "Update service" start= disabled
  • Mac: launchctl unload -w /Library/LaunchDaemons/PT.updd.plist

On Android, the updater is built into the app and cannot be turned off on its own, and it installs only if the user taps to accept, so Eye did not send updates to Android devices. Removing the app is the only fix there.

To check a network, defenders can look for the two updater files, Updater.exe on Windows and PT.updd on Mac, and for traffic to the web addresses in Eye's write-up, which lists all 20 domains and the file hashes.

item.title: Google Says Gmail and Photos Data Shared With AI Search Could Be Used for Targeted Ads (2026)
item.description:
Google has updated its privacy policy to spell out that using personalized artificial intelligence (AI) features in Search or Gemini could allow the company to serve targeted ads to users based on their activity on other connected Google services.

"You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service," reads a policy update effective October 16, 2026.

"For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads."

Google also notes in its revised policy that "We don't show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos, unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads."

News of the policy update was first reported by Android Authority.

Personal Intelligence, unveiled by Google in Gemini in January 2026, allows users to connect other services like Gmail, Google Photos, and YouTube as a way to provide tailored answers in combination with their chat history preferences.

The feature is currently rolling out as a beta to eligible users over the age of 18 globally, except in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, the U.K., and Nigeria.

It's worth noting that the policy states it doesn't use content from Gmail, Drive, or Photos to personalize ads by default. However, that changes should users opt to share photos or emails with AI Mode and other Search tools via the Personal Intelligence feature.

In other words, if users interact with AI Mode or Gemini while Personal Intelligence is enabled, the data that informs those answers (i.e., content from Gmail or Photos) could be used as a signal to serve targeted ads. The privacy policy aims to make it clear that feeding personal data into its AI tools could contribute to ad personalization.

Users should be mindful of the privacy trade-off when connecting their apps to enable AI features. Those who prefer to opt out can do so by selecting the apps they want to disconnect from Personal Intelligence or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings ("www.google[.]com/search-personalization").

In January 2026, OpenAI began showing ads to logged-in adult U.S. users in both the free and ChatGPT Go tiers, while emphasizing that users' data and conversations are protected and never sold to advertisers. It has also said the ads do not influence responses from the chatbot, and that users are in control of the experience.

Earlier this week, the AI company said it's expanded advertising on ChatGPT to 26 more countries, ​bringing the total to 89. This includes 14 more ​Latin American countries and several markets across Europe, Africa, and Asia.

"We keep conversations private from advertisers and do not sell customer data," OpenAI stressed. "Ads in ChatGPT are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT's answers, and advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides."

item.title: Leaked LiteLLM Master Key Let Attackers Steal GitHub Tokens and Hijack Release Pipeline (2026)
item.description:
LiteLLM on Friday revealed that an Agent Platform master key accidentally published to a public GitHub repository in late May 2026 ultimately allowed the threat actor to push a malicious version of the popular Python package.

"On May 27, 2026, a configuration file was committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repository which inadvertently contained the master key to a deployment of the LiteLLM Agent Platform, an open source tool we use for orchestrating agents," LiteLLM's Oliver Jensen and Mateo Wang said.

"The error was quickly identified, the commit force-pushed over, and we identified the exposed keys as requiring revocation. However, key revocation did not occur for the master key."

LiteLLM said the unknown attacker (operating from "69.48.229[.]143") used this unrevoked key on October 10, 2026, to gain access to the Agent Platform and extracted a GitHub CLI OAuth token the service was configured with to allow self-hosted cloud agents to file pull requests to GitHub repositories.

The token, per the developers of the open-source large language model (LLM) gateway, was "not scoped down" and associated with its GitHub organization owner's account.

Gaining access to the token allowed the attacker to possess owner-level access to all repositories across the organization and perform additional credential exfiltration. The sequence of actions performed by the threat actor following this step is as follows -

  • October 10, 2026, between 10:11 and 10:12 p.m. UTC: Author commits into throwaway branches on internal repositories to run workflows (BerriAI/litellm and BerriAI/litellm-auto) designed to acquire GitHub CLI Oauth tokens associated with two engineers with maintainer privileges via an attacker-controlled webhook[.]site endpoint. The two runs are deleted minutes later.
  • October 21, 2026, between 10:08 and 11:08 a.m. UTC: Override branch protection and alter the release pipeline with the source set to the lookalike repository "Berri-AI/litellm" rather than "BerriAI/litellm."
  • October 21, 2026, between 11:39 and 11:40 a.m. UTC: LiteLLM version 1.107.0 gets published to PyPI on
  • October 21, 2026, 11:46 a.m. UTC: Docker Hub and GHCR images are published.
  • October 21, 2026, between 11:53 and 11:54 a.m. UTC: Production and staging run records are deleted.
  • October 21, 2026, 12:06 p.m. UTC: Supply chain attack reported by Upwind researcher Lidor Machluf.
  • October 21, 2026, 1:23 p.m. UTC: PyPI quarantines LiteLLM version 1.107.0.
  • October 21, 2025, 2:20 p.m. UTC: Docker Hub tags v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable are removed or repointed to verified clean images.

"In typical operation, building and publishing a release requires being kicked off by an authorized engineer and being approved by a special account locked to a physical device in our office," LiteLLM said.

Leaked master key in May 2026

"This restriction was relaxed earlier this week to accommodate the temporary push for more frequent releases and bugfix backports, allowing any two engineers to trigger and approve a release. As such, the threat actor used one of the tokens to trigger the release (after having repointed the deployer to their malicious repository), and another to approve it."

In addition, the project maintainers noted that the threat actor could have very well loosened this restriction (or removed it entirely) themselves given that they were already in possession of a token belonging to an organization owner. It's suspected that this was not done to evade detection.

LiteLLM also said the workflows are designed to identify and exfiltrate additional keys and tokens, specifically focusing on upstream inference API tokens. In response to the incident, the company said it's working to revoke each and every token associated with every internal system and vendor platform.

More Details About the Workflows Emerge

Socket, which published its own investigation into the malicious workflows, said it recovered two malicious commits that each added a workflow at ".github/workflows/cache.yml." The first commit was made on October 10, 2026, at 10:11:45 p.m. UTC. It was followed by a second commit on October 12.

"Neither commit was pushed to a branch that still exists," Socket security researcher Karlo Zanki said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "Both were pushed to short-lived branches named ci-tmp-<hex> that were created, used, and deleted within minutes, which is why the activity leaves almost nothing behind in the repository's ordinary history."

According to the application security firm's analysis of the repository's activity log records, both commits rely on a legitimate commit as the branch base to make the push look seemingly harmless -

  • Create a throwaway branch named "ci-tmp-<hex>" (namely, ci-tmp-a351cc and ci-tmp-4d8517) from a recent legitimate commit on the repository.
  • Push a commit adding ".github/workflows/cache.yml" with the same subject, "ci: bump cache config."
  • The workflow is configured to be run every time a commit or tag is pushed (i.e., "on: [push]"), causing it to be triggered.
  • Delete the branch.

Both workflows, as highlighted by LiteLLM, are equipped to harvest GitHub tokens and API keys for the organization's Linear workspace, LiteLLM deployment, and Together AI, along with the identifier and signing key of a GitHub App.

The October 12 run extends the collection to more secrets, including API keys for Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Tavily, and GitGuardian's secret-scanning tenant. It also captures Playwright storage state, PostgreSQL database information (connection string, account name, password), Redis endpoint address, port, and authentication password.

The data gathered from the two workflows is exfiltrated to two different webhook[.]site endpoints -

  • webhook[.]site/65a42464-3cfa-4b02-a18c-17a6d7b86f37
  • webhook[.]site/4da03473-a3e7-4dc2-a087-9c564b4208e1

"A GitHub token and a GitHub App private key are credentials for the platform hosting the repository, not for a third-party service," Zanki said. "GITGUARDIAN_API_KEY is a credential for the secret-scanning platform itself, which gives an attacker visibility into, and potentially control over, the alerts that would surface this activity.

"E2E_LINEAR_STORAGE_STATE_B64 is serialized browser session state used by Playwright for end-to-end tests; a valid storage state permits authenticated access to the associated Linear account without a password and without satisfying multi-factor authentication."

The findings rule out LiteLLM's initial hypothesis that the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens were stolen from the logs of an internal LiteLLM deployment. "The investigation was a process in which we continually learned additional information, meaning some of our assumptions and beliefs were later proven to be inaccurate or incomplete," Jensen acknowledged.

What the Malicious Version of the Package Does

Multiple reports have revealed that the files bundled with LiteLLM version 1.107.0 are engineered to execute automatically when Python starts, even if an application did not import LiteLLM.

The malware features two execution paths: a credential harvesting module that targets authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, and web browsers, and a Unix-oriented backdoor that's launched as a background process to fetch and execute arbitrary code supplied by the attacker every one hour.

Compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 execution flow

The stealer also collects system information, SSH files, Git and GitLab credentials and tokens, environment variables, and tokens associated with npm, PyPI, pip, Yarn, Maven, Gradle, Composer, RubyGems, and Cargo. item.title: Brotli Decoder Flaw Behind Node.js RCE Also Affects Bun, Python and Other Widely Used Software (2026)
item.description:
A memory-corruption flaw in Google's Brotli decoder sits in many programs that unpack Brotli-compressed data, among them Bun, the Python Brotli and brotlicffi packages, and Envoy proxies set up to decompress Brotli.

Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, the flaw allows crafted compressed data to overwrite past the end of a buffer and corrupt a program's memory, potentially causing a crash, a memory leak, or the execution of attacker-controlled code.

Imperva researchers have shown that code can run on one unpatched Node.js build. The same has not been demonstrated on the other software, and no real-world attacks have been reported.

The flaw was first disclosed on October 21, when Node.js and Google shipped fixes, and more have followed product by product since. Because the bug is in Google's decoder and each program ships its own copy of it, every one has to update that copy on its own.

Brotli is a compression format from Google, used across the web to shrink pages and other traffic. The bug is in the C code that unpacks a Brotli stream, so it travels into anything that reuses that code, from language runtimes to proxies to Python packages.

Which Software Is Affected

Product Affected Fixed in Exposed when
Google Brotli (C library) 1.0.3 to 1.2.0 1.0.10, 1.1.1, 1.2.1 code decodes untrusted Brotli
Node.js 22.x, 24.x, 26.x before the fix; 20.x and older (end of life) 22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1 fetch() of a br response, or Express or body-parser br bodies
Bun 1.4.3 and earlier 1.4.4 fetch() of a br response, or node:zlib
Envoy 1.39.2, 1.38.5, 1.37.7, 1.36.11 1.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, 1.37.8, 1.36.12 only if the Brotli decompressor is configured
Istio 1.31.0 to 1.31.1, 1.30.0 to 1.30.5, 1.29.0 to 1.29.8 1.31.2, 1.30.6, 1.29.9 only if Brotli decompression is enabled
Python Brotli 1.2.0 and earlier 1.2.1 installed, and an HTTP client decodes br
Python brotlicffi 1.2.0.x and earlier 1.2.1.0 installed, and an HTTP client decodes br
cdxgen standalone binaries and images, 13.4.0 and 12.8.8 and earlier 13.5.0, 12.8.9 standalone binary or image scanning untrusted input

A program is exposed only if it decodes Brotli data that someone else controls. For Node.js and Bun, that happens when the built-in fetch() reads a response sent with Content-Encoding: br, or when request-body code such as Express 5 and body-parser 2 unpacks a Brotli upload. A plain Node.js HTTP server does not decode request bodies on its own.

Envoy and Istio are affected only when Brotli decompression is enabled, for example, through an Envoy filter. Where it is off, the flaw cannot be reached.

In Python, the risk comes from the Brotli or brotlicffi package being installed at all. Once either is present, HTTP clients such as requests, urllib3, httpx, and aiohttp decode Brotli responses on their own, so an application can be exposed without ever importing Brotli in its own code.

A web application firewall helps only so far. Vercel, which added firewall rules on the day of disclosure, said those rules do not cover "responses your functions fetch from other servers." For that path, only updating the runtime or library closes the hole.

How far the flaw can be pushed depends on the software. Imperva's Red Team, which calls its work Node2Shell, ran attacker-supplied code on an unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 build for Linux on ARM64, delivering it both as a fetched response and as an Express request body. The exploit took several tries, has not been released, and was not tested on other builds.

OpenAI, whose Codex Security team reported the flaw, describes it as enabling unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli and lists Node.js, Bun, and Envoy as affected software. In its account, the flaw works both ways:

an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as "curl --compressed") could be taken over by a malicious server.

No in-the-wild exploitation has been reported. CISA's October 23 assessment recorded exploitation as "none" and automation as "no," and Red Hat said there is no reliable public proof-of-concept for running code.

Severity ratings differ by who is scoring. Google, which assigned the CVE, rates it 9.2, or critical, on the CVSS 4.0 scale. Node.js calls it high, and Red Hat rates it 8.1, or important.

The fix has an unusual history. The change that closes the flaw was added to Brotli's source code on February 27, but no new Brotli release carried it until October 21. OpenAI said the root cause "was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn't known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli."

Node.js credits Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer of OpenAI's Codex Security for reporting the flaw, and maintainers Matteo Collina and Antoine du Hamel for the fix.

What to Do Now

Update to a fixed version from the table above, then restart the service and rebuild any container image, because a running process keeps the old decoder until it restarts.

Where you cannot update yet, stop decoding untrusted Brotli. OpenAI's disclosure page and the security firm Aikido both recommend:

  • Reject incoming requests with Content-Encoding: br before any proxy or parser decodes the body.
  • Turn off automatic Brotli decoding in HTTP clients, and reject Brotli responses before they are decoded.
  • In Python, uninstall the Brotli and brotlicffi packages so clients fall back to gzip and deflate.

Dropping br from the Accept-Encoding header does not help on its own, because a server can send Brotli whatever the client asks for. For Node.js, no workaround has been published, so updating the runtime is the only fix.

System packages are being fixed at different times. Debian fixed its brotli package for Debian 13 (trixie) on October 23 in version 1.1.0-2+deb13u1. Amazon Linux 2023 still listed its brotli and Node.js 24 packages as pending a fix as of October 22.

Dependency scanners may not flag the Python packages yet. The CVE record names Google's Brotli repository, not the PyPI packages, and GitHub's advisory still lists no affected package, which is what Dependabot reads. Advisory entries for the two Python packages, PYSEC-2026-4322 and PYSEC-2026-4323, were added on October 23, so check the installed versions manually as well.
